 Commentary 
 Opinion | Local news is strong in Maine. Coverage of the 2026 campaign proved it.
 Rather than being a sign of the news business’ collapse, the journalism produced by national and local outlets is the product of a thriving ecosystem
 Voters fill out their ballots then wait in line to put in a counting machine Tuesday morning at the Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley in Gardiner. (Joe Phelan/Portland Press Herald)
 By:
 Tom Wiley and Stefanie Manning 
 November 19, 2026 
 -->
 -->
 As local media executives, we’re used to criticism of our newsrooms, usually from politicians, business owners and readers. An essential part of our jobs is listening to and learning from our critics. In the sometimes messy, often imperfect quest to unearth and deliver news to our communities, we sometimes get things wrong.
 However, it’s frustrating when that criticism comes from our own industry through a lens that doesn’t capture the full picture of what’s currently happening in local journalism. Too often, facts are ignored or manipulated in service of an incorrect and damaging narrative about the news business and how it’s changing.
 That’s why we’d like to address a piece Poynter published last week with the headline, “National news outlets landed the biggest stories of the 2026 campaign. That’s a problem.” 
 The piece was built on conventional wisdom about local newsrooms in decline. It ignored facts and explanations that might have produced a different and more nuanced understanding of how politics gets covered in states today. And it represents a pattern of industry publications stuffing every observation into a narrative of collapse.
 Consider the article’s premise: Local newsrooms are “hollowed out”; the journalists who remain live in fear of subscription cancellations; and the result is a “drift toward the ‘nationalization’ of deep political reporting.” The author specifically cites coverage of the U.S. Senate race in Maine, where the National Trust for Local News and its state affiliate, the Maine Trust for Local News, publish 11 newspapers, including the Portland Press Herald.
 There’s no doubt that local news faces serious challenges. However, newsrooms in the state of Maine are not “hollowed out.” Our organization is proud to employ more than 100 journalists covering a geography with about 1.2 million of Maine’s 1.4 million people. Our peers in the state include thriving newsrooms at the Bangor Daily News, Maine Monitor and Maine Public — to name a few. We enjoy strong collaborations with them all, including this election season.
 Contrary to the author’s assertion, we do not suffer from “waning” subscriptions. Sure, our print circulation has been declining, but our digital subscriptions in Portland are up more than 10% so far this year. We added thousands of new subscribers across the state during the campaign, especially in the weeks leading up to the primary and general elections. Monthly average users increased year over year, with audience growth extending beyond the election cycle and onto more platforms than ever. We’re diversifying revenue away from advertising to events, donations and syndication revenue.
 It’s flat wrong to say that fear of losing advertisers or subscribers impacts the news judgment of our current editors. There will never be a day when an NTLN newsroom — in Maine, or in Georgia, Vermont and Colorado, where we also operate — allows narrow commercial interests to influence its news decisions.
 So how then do we explain why many of the biggest political moments in Maine this year came only when the national media broke big stories? Why isn’t this a “serious underlying problem,” as the Poynter article suggests?
 We celebrate the outstanding work of journalists at The New York Times, ProPublica or Politico. In fact, we published some of their stories, including on the front pages of our newspapers. We delivered those high-impact scoops to voters in Maine, because, just as we collaborate with media in the state, we’re part of a broader media ecosystem that aims to serve our audiences with the information they need to make good decisions, regardless of the source. ProPublica’s model indeed assumes local outlets will want to publish their reporting. And some of the national reporters who broke big stories in Maine started their careers in the state.
 A more nuanced understanding of what’s happening in American journalism today would reflect not what Poynter’s piece calls the “‘nationalization’ of deep political reporting” but rather the nationalization of state politics. There are two reasons for this. First, in a midterm election cycle, national politics plays out in competitive states, like Maine, that make up the front line in the battle for control of the U.S. Senate. Second, with the rise of cable television, podcasts and social media, when a national outlet like The New York Times publishes a story about a state race, it gets mainlined into the national political conversation.
 That’s not to say there aren’t also many important stories being broken locally and driving the conversation among voters. The Maine Trust’s political coverage this year included plenty of scoops, like reporting that Sen. Susan Collins’ allies were still working with operatives linked to the scheme detailed by ProPublica or investigating whether a member of the Bush family met the residency requirements to run for governor. Led by a four-person politics team , we exhaustively covered the races for Maine’s open seats for governor and the second congressional district. We provided open access to a voter guide , used by 50,000 readers, that provided profiles of candidates in 311 statewide and local races. We sponsored gubernatorial and U.S. Senate debates with Maine Public and a local television station. And we conducted multiple polls in conjunction with our partners at Siena Research Institute and, yes, the New York Times.
 We aren’t alone. Our collaborators at the Bangor Daily News have had an investigative team since 2013. That team reported on the web of ties between Collins and the leader of a super PAC supporting her. It also revealed that Troy Jackson hadn’t reported income from logging since 2012, despite his political brand as a logger. At Maine Public, a team of experienced political reporters provided insight and context on everything from Jackson’s history in Maine to the pervasiveness of dark money in the U.S. Senate race. They also amplified ProPublica’s investigation into Collins on air and online. The Maine Monitor detailed how a new campaign finance website has been plagued by problems and reviewed the health care proposals from the leading candidates for governor.
 During this same period, the Maine Trust consistently dug deep and broke news on the issues that matter most to Mainers. These are also issues that shaped the election. Take the skyrocketing cost of living in the state, detailed in our series “Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine.” Or the increase in ICE activity that came to a crescendo with the July shooting of Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero. We were first to identify the ICE agent who killed him. We interviewed Guerrero’s family , chronicled the ICE agent’s troubled past and were in the middle of daily protests from an angry community. After The New York Times last week published a great investigation about the agent’s history of anti-immigrant views, one of the story’s reporters graciously cited the Press Herald’s “extraordinary work” unearthing the agent’s history. Again, that’s the ecosystem in action.
 As this evidence shows, what’s happening in Maine is the opposite of demise. We’re building a sustainable future for local journalism. Yes, that requires us to evolve. That means investing in digital products, developing new revenue streams, collaborating across newsrooms and making difficult decisions about where our resources can have the greatest impact. As we do so, we should be measured not simply by the structures we’ve maintained from the past, but by the quality, reach and relevance of the journalism we’re producing today.
 Our work is important, and so it should be scrutinized. When we screw up, we should be held accountable — just like those we cover. But when the journalism press’ worldview is one of inescapable demise — with the occasional success story framed as a quirky outlier — it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Readers start to believe it. Sources start to believe it. Supporters start to believe it.
 Mainers were well served this election, by our newsrooms, our peers and the national outlets that reported alongside us. That’s not a warning sign. That’s what a working news ecosystem looks like.
 Tom Wiley 
 Chief Executive Officer, National Trust for Local News 
 Stefanie Manning 
 President and Publisher, Maine Trust for Local News
